practical.title: INTENSIVE Lab — Implement and Compare Bubble, Selection, and Insertion Sorts (C)

coachingPrompts: What do you predict will happen before you run it?
What evidence shows that your change worked?
Can you explain the result in your own words?

teachingPlaylist.title: Run and read the starter sorting program
teachingPlaylist.description: Compile the provided main.c and observe how it prints the original and three sorted arrays. This confirms the baseline behavior.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Confirm the starter program runs and that all three algorithms produce the same final sorted result from identical inputs.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Let's compile and run the provided starter program. I'll speak the important printed lines as they appear. Predict the final sequence then run the command. Notice the program prints the original array, then labels each algorithm's output — this label helps you trace which function produced which output.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Run: gcc main.c -o sorts && ./sorts and observe Original array then three Sorted array lines showing ascending numbers.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You have a small unsorted list and want to see three sorting algorithms operate on identical data.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Before running, say aloud what the sorted sequence will be. Then run the program and compare to your prediction.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Thinking each sort modifies the same array variable; the starter code copies the array for each sort so that's not happening here.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You ran the starter file and verified each algorithm produces the same ascending output. We will now make a small, deliberate change to the array to see cause-and-effect.
codeSteps: Open main.c and locate original_arr initializer.

teachingPlaylist.title: Change the input to a short array and run again
teachingPlaylist.description: Edit the original_arr initializer to a 6-element array so you can more easily step through traces later.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: See how a small change in input affects algorithm behavior and make predictions about operations.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Now change the initializer to a short 6-element array. This single-line edit focuses your attention. After compiling, observe that the three sorted results still match. Predict which sort will do less work for nearly-sorted inputs.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Edit the initializer and run gcc main.c -o sorts && ./sorts. Compare predicted sorted list to the program output.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You need to debug sorting behavior on a concise example.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Change the initializer to {5,1,4,2,8,0}. Run the program. Note the printed sorted arrays.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Forgetting to save the file before compiling; or editing a different copy of the file.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You made a tiny change (1 line), recompiled, and confirmed the algorithms still produce consistent sorted output. Next we'll add tracing output so you can see the algorithms step-by-step.
codeSteps: Open main.c and replace the original_arr initializer with {5, 1, 4, 2, 8, 0}.
Save file and run gcc main.c -o sorts.

teachingPlaylist.title: Add tracing to see each swap/insert
teachingPlaylist.description: Replace main.c with an augmented traced version that prints a 'Trace:' line whenever a swap or insertion occurs.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Visualize how each algorithm manipulates the array step-by-step so you can map algorithm textbook descriptions to concrete actions.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: We're adding a small trace underscore print helper and then calling it after every swap or after each insertion. These textual traces are your terminal 'color blocks'. Read them in sequence to see how elements move.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: After replacing file content, compile and run. Look for lines starting with 'Trace:' for each algorithm.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You want to debug or teach sorting behavior and need to see intermediate steps.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Replace main.c with the traced version, compile, then run. Follow the trace lines and map them to the algorithm descriptions.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Printing traces too often can clutter the output. We print only at swaps or after insertions to keep output meaningful.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You added a tracing helper and saw how each algorithm changes the array step-by-step. Next we'll verify algorithm behavior against edge cases.
codeSteps: Overwrite main.c with the provided traced implementation (use the cat > main.c << 'EOF' ... EOF sequence).
Run ./sorts and inspect 'Trace:' lines for Bubble, Selection, and Insertion.

teachingPlaylist.title: Verify edge cases and add counters (optional)
teachingPlaylist.description: Test already-sorted, reverse-sorted, and duplicates. Optionally add comparison and swap counters to each implementation and print them to compare relative work.
teachingPlaylist.learningGoal: Confirm algorithm behavior on edge cases and quantify relative work with counters.
teachingPlaylist.narratorScript: Run the traced program on three important edge cases. Observe how bubble sort quickly exits when input is already sorted, how reverse-sorted triggers many swaps, and how duplicates reveal whether an algorithm is stable.
teachingPlaylist.workedExample: Change initializer to {0,1,2,4,5,8} then to {8,5,4,2,1,0} then to {2,3,2,1,3,1}, compiling and running each time.
teachingPlaylist.scenario: You must ensure your sorting code works correctly for tricky inputs and quantify cost.
teachingPlaylist.learnerPrompt: Run the three tests. Then (optional) add integer counters 'comparisons' and 'swaps' to each function and increment them at each comparison and swap; print the final counts after each sort.
teachingPlaylist.commonMistake: Assuming equal final output implies equal internal work; counters reveal differing numbers of comparisons and swaps.
teachingPlaylist.recap: You verified correctness across edge cases and learned how to instrument code to measure internal work. This prepares you to reason about Big O in practice.
codeSteps: Edit the array initializer to each edge case in turn and recompile.
Observe trace output and final sorted arrays.
Optional: add integer counters and print them after each sort to compare work.

tasks.title: Scene 1 — OBSERVE & UNDERSTAND: Run the provided starter program
tasks.narratorGuide: Connect: We'll use the exact starter file main.c. Observe: compile and run it and read the printed output. Change: none yet. Test: look for the original array, then three sorted outputs. Explain: each algorithm should print the same ascending sequence; they differ in the way they get there. Pause: predict whether the three final lists will be identical before running. Worked example: compile now with gcc main.c -o sorts && ./sorts. Real-world example: sorting a shortlist of user IDs before display. Teacher question: What do you expect the sorted output to be? Expected observation: each 'Sorted array:' line shows numbers in ascending order. Pause before continuing.

tasks.title: Scene 2 — MODIFY & EXPERIMENT: Change the input array (1-2 lines)
tasks.narratorGuide: CONNECT: We've seen the full 10-element run. OBSERVE: make a minimal change — replace the initializer with six elements. CHANGE: Edit exactly one line: the initializer. TEST: Recompile and run to see the smaller example. EXPLAIN: Smaller arrays let you mentally step through each algorithm. EXTEND: Try other small arrays with duplicates next. Worked example: replace the initializer and run gcc main.c -o sorts && ./sorts. Real-world example: quick debug on a short input to confirm algorithm correctness before scaling. Teacher question: Which algorithm will likely show the fewest operations on this nearly random 6-element array? Expected observation: all algorithms still give the same final sorted list but the number of internal operations differs. Pause before continuing.

tasks.title: Scene 3 — BUILD & INTEGRATE: Add a tracing mode to show comparisons and swaps
tasks.narratorGuide: CONNECT: You've run the baseline and seen final outputs. OBSERVE: now we add tracing so you see intermediate states. CHANGE: replace main.c content with the provided traced version (full file below). TEST: compile and run. EXPLAIN: look for lines beginning with Trace: to follow swaps. EXTEND: try tracing a reverse-sorted array. Worked example: replace the file, compile with gcc main.c -o sorts && ./sorts. Real-world example: tracing helps debug why a sort fails on certain inputs. Teacher question: When you see 'Trace: Bubble swapped', what does that tell you about the relative size of neighboring elements? Expected observation: multiple trace lines showing swaps until the array becomes sorted. Pause before continuing.

tasks.title: Scene 4 — VERIFY & EXTEND: Edge cases and optional counters
tasks.narratorGuide: CONNECT: Use the traced program from Scene 3. OBSERVE: run three variants by editing the initializer line to one of the edge-case arrays. CHANGE: swap the initializer and re-run. TEST: look at trace outputs and counts (if you add counters). EXPLAIN: note bubble sort's early exit on already-sorted input and selection sort's repeated comparisons even when sorted. EXTEND: (Optional) add integer variables comparisons and swaps counters in each sort and increment at comparison/swap points, then print results after each sort. Worked example: edit original_arr to reverse-sorted and run. Real-world example: ensure sort correctness for inputs like logs with repeated timestamps. Teacher question: Which algorithm showed the fewest trace steps on the already-sorted array and why? Expected observation: Bubble (with early-exit) produces no swaps; insertion also does minimal work; selection still scans. Pause before continuing.
